Header:
Date: 2026-11-17
Start time: 14:05 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Sarah (BrightByte PM), Carlos (BrightByte Eng), Priya (BrightByte Security)

Summary:
Quick weekly checkpoint for the BrightByte POC focusing on app integration: SDK usage, function/tool calling, structured JSON outputs, and tuned prompt results. Reviewed a small benchmark run (p95 latency + token cost), discussed a couple of failure modes (truncated JSON, partial function invocations), and agreed next steps: share docs and schedule engineer pairing.

Topics covered:
- SDK integration patterns (redwood-js + python SDK notes)
- Function calling and tool invocations (webhook vs local adapter)
- Structured output schema stability and validation failures
- Performance numbers: p50/p95, batching, KV cache hit rate

Action items (mentioned in call):
- Alex to send annotated prompt set and eval spreadsheet
- Evan to share KV-cache tuning doc, quantization recs
- Carlos to run a scaled benchmark and upload logs
- Priya to confirm KMS + data residency constraints

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick agenda: run through the small benchmark results you sent, discuss the integration snags, and set action items. Sound good?
[00:18] Sarah (BrightByte): Yep, thanks Alex. we had two main blockers last week — truncated JSON coming back from function calls, and some surprising latency spikes when we hit bursts.
[00:32] Evan (Redwood): Ok, can you remind me which SDK you're using in the app? is that redwood-js or the Python wrapper?
[00:41] Carlos (BrightByte): We're on redwood-js in prod-like staging, with a tiny node adapter. we also have a Python microservice that calls the API for analytics.
[00:50] Evan (Redwood): Cool. two things to call out: streaming + structured output patterns behave a bit differently. If you're not reading the full stream you can hit partial JSON issues. Also, function calling can be interrupted if the model falls back to a different variant mid-response.
[01:12] Sarah (BrightByte): That sounds like what we saw. sometimes the UI only awaited the first chunk and parsed it, which choked on incomplete JSON.
[01:20] Alex (Redwood): Right. typical pattern we recommend: either collect the full stream and validate against the schema before surface, or use the function-calling contract which signals intent and returns structured args. Evan, can you give the short rec?
[01:33] Evan (Redwood): Yeah. two practical options: 1) switch to the SDK helper that buffers and emits a single parsed JSON object, that's a 5-line change in redwood-js; or 2) keep streaming but include a robust JSON assemble/repair step client-side — we can share a snippet. Also, enable the SDK's strict_schema option so the runtime rejects nonconforming output.
[01:57] Carlos (BrightByte): Where is that strict_schema flag documented? we missed that in the quickstart.
[02:04] Evan (Redwood): I'll drop the link and a short example. it's in the SDK reference under "structured_output" — older quickstarts might not highlight it.
[02:10] Sarah (BrightByte): Thanks. on the latency spikes: we ran a 1k request burst test and saw p95 jump from 280ms to 1.2s during peak. any tuning we should try?
[02:22] Alex (Redwood): Do you recall if those bursts were hitting the same model variant or did the router fail over to a cheaper fallback?
[02:30] Carlos (BrightByte): I think there was an automatic fallback to a quantized variant when capacity was tight. we weren't pinning model version.
[02:37] Evan (Redwood): That explains it. fallback can increase CPU-bound latency. For consistent p95 you can either: pin to Dedicated capacity (if you have reserved GPUs), or configure routing policy to prefer the unquantized variant for latency-sensitive routes. There's also batching/queue settings — if your per-request tokens are small, continuous batching can help but it increases tail latency slightly.
[03:00] Sarah (BrightByte): We're trying to balance cost — Dedicated is a big step. can you share the pricing bands again for Dedicated vs hosted burst?
[03:10] Alex (Redwood): Will share. For the pilot we recommended a small dedicated pool with burst to hosted for overflow — it's a middle ground. I'll attach the numbers after the call.
[03:20] Priya (BrightByte): Quick security check — on the logs we saw token payloads in traces. we need to ensure PII is not stored and confirm KMS options for Private.
[03:30] Evan (Redwood): Understood. Redwood's Private and Dedicated both support customer-managed KMS and can be configured to redact or avoid storing raw prompts in long-term logs. For hosted, we have configurable retention and audit logs; I'll include the SOC2 section and the KMS integration doc.
[03:48] Sarah (BrightByte): Great. another question: function calling — we're invoking an internal tool to fetch patient meta-data via a webhook. is it safer to call internal services or to route data through Redwood tools?
[04:02] Evan (Redwood): Best practice: keep PII inside your VPC and surface only non-sensitive context to LLM. For webhooks, use signed tokens and short-lived credentials. If you use Redwood Private, you can run the connector inside your network. We'll share a pattern doc.
[04:18] Carlos (BrightByte): On structured output — we have a schema for the tool result and sometimes the model returns extra fields or nested arrays that break our parser. any tips?
[04:28] Alex (Redwood): Two levels: model-side guidance and runtime enforcement. Model-side: use explicit instructions + a handful of examples to bias output. Runtime: strict schema validation + a fallback sanitizer that maps unknown fields. We'll share examples.
[04:45] Evan (Redwood): Also consider using function-calling where the model returns typed args instead of freeform JSON, reduces mismatch. For nested arrays, include a post-processor that flattens into canonical form.
[05:00] Sarah (BrightByte): Ok. can you also comment on quantization recs? we tried int8 and saw quality dip on certain prompt templates.
[05:10] Evan (Redwood): Yep. Int8 can introduce subtle tokenization shifts for domain-specific terminology. If you have sensitive clinical terms, keep those routes on unquantized or bfloat16 variants. For most user-facing features int8 is fine; but for extraction/structured tasks we often recommend bfloat16 or q4f16. I'll provide a recommended mapping doc.
[05:32] Carlos (BrightByte): That mapping doc would be helpful. Also, any SDK flags to reduce token inflation? we're seeing some prompts expand in generation.
[05:41] Alex (Redwood): Prompt engineering + model temperature + max tokens. There's also a per-route post-filter we can enable to trim filler tokens. We can annotate the sample prompts you shared and return a 'tightened' set.
[05:55] Sarah (BrightByte): You mentioned a small benchmark earlier — can we go over the numbers you saw?
[06:02] Alex (Redwood): Right — Evan, do you want to read the quick numbers from the run BrightByte sent?
[06:09] Evan (Redwood): Sure. The sample run (1k calls, mixed sizes) — p50: 210ms, p95: 280ms when pinned; but with fallback events p95 jumped to 1.2s. Token cost averaged 0.9 cents per 1k tokens for the quantized variant, and 2.1 cents per 1k tokens for the unquantized baseline. KV-cache hit rate looked about 22% on the short-prefix cache, so there's room to improve with better prefixing and shared cache keys.
[06:44] Sarah (BrightByte): Ok that aligns with what we saw. what's our recommended next step to reduce cost without worsening p95?
[06:52] Evan (Redwood): A few tactics: increase cache hit rate via canonicalization of prompts, enable longer prefix cache TTL for common flows, and selectively quantize lower importance routes while keeping extraction/structured-output routes on higher-precision variants. Also, batch similar low-latency calls at the gateway to improve throughput.
[07:14] Carlos (BrightByte): For cache keys — we have user ids in the prompt. Should we strip or hash them?
[07:20] Evan (Redwood): Hash user-specific fields or move them to metadata that's not part of the cached prompt key. That tends to increase hit rate. We'll share a sample canonicalization script.
[07:31] Alex (Redwood): Quick interruption — we also saw one example of the model calling the wrong tool when two tools have similar names. There's a small disambiguation trick in the tool descriptor — add explicit examples and stronger name hints.
[07:44] Sarah (BrightByte): Oh yeah, we had a "lookupPatient" and "lookupPatientLegacy" and sometimes the model chose the legacy.
[07:50] Evan (Redwood): Rename with clearer verbs e.g., "patient_lookup_v2" and add an example invocation. That reduces mis-selection.
[07:58] Carlos (BrightByte): Noted. On the SDK side, we hit an EPIPE error occasionally from the node adapter during high concurrency. Any pointers?
[08:06] Evan (Redwood): EPIPE usually means socket closed server-side under load — likely upstream connection re-use config in node. Use the SDK's connection pool settings and increase keepalive. Also, bump the HTTP agent max sockets. We'll paste a recommended config.
[08:22] Sarah (BrightByte): Good. security follow-up — Priya, do you want to mention the audit asks?
[08:28] Priya (BrightByte): Sure. we need to confirm that request-level audit logs can be exported to our SIEM, and that the Hosted option can meet our retention policy of 90 days for non-PII traces. Also KMS for keys and optional HSM for the Private deployment.
[08:45] Evan (Redwood): We support log export to your SIEM via S3 sink + loghooks. For KMS/HSM we can detail the Private deployment offering; hosted supports key encryption with customer-managed keys in some tiers. I'll include the SOC2/ISO artifacts.
[08:59] Alex (Redwood): ok, circling back to actionable tuning — Evan, you mentioned a KV-cache tuning doc. what will that include?
[09:08] Evan (Redwood): It'll have: cache key design, TTL recommendations by route type, sample canonicalization scripts (node + python), and a short checklist for cache warmup. Also quantization compatibility notes with cache (don't mix incompatible kernel variants).
[09:26] Carlos (BrightByte): Cache warmup — can we seed the cache from historical queries?
[09:31] Evan (Redwood): Yes. You can pre-populate prefix cache via a batch job. We usually recommend warmup jobs during low-traffic windows.
[09:38] Sarah (BrightByte): Let's talk about the engineer pairing. we want Evan or someone from infra to pair with Carlos to reproduce the EPIPE and the JSON truncation flow.
[09:48] Alex (Redwood): Great. suggested slot is Friday 11/20 at 11am PST. Carlos, does that work?
[09:53] Carlos (BrightByte): Yes that works.
[09:55] Priya (BrightByte): On data residency, we need to ensure the EU region is used for EU patient records. Can we pin region by dataset?
[10:03] Evan (Redwood): You can set per-route region preference; for strict residency we recommend Private or a dedicated regional deployment. We'll add that to the migration notes.
[10:15] Sarah (BrightByte): One more nit: sometimes the model hallucinated an identifier format in the output; it's small but causes downstream parse errors. any deterministic mitigation?
[10:25] Evan (Redwood): Stronger schema + regex validators post-emit. Also include examples of correct and incorrect outputs in the prompt to bias generation. If it's critical, put that piece in a function that validates and rejects on mismatch.
[10:39] Alex (Redwood): Alright, let's capture the concrete next steps (I'll read them out): 1) Alex sends tightened prompt set and annotated failures by Thu 11/19. 2) Evan shares KV-cache tuning guide + quantization mapping by Fri 11/20. 3) Carlos runs 10k job and uploads logs by Tue 11/24. 4) Priya confirms KMS/residency asks by Sat 11/21. 5) Engineer pairing scheduled Fri 11/20 11:00 PST. Everyone ok?
[11:08] Sarah (BrightByte): Yes. that matches our expectations.
[11:12] Carlos (BrightByte): Yup. quick question — can you also include a short script to reassemble streamed JSON? we have an internal lib but want to compare.
[11:20] Evan (Redwood): I'll paste one in the follow-up doc (Node + Python).

[11:40] Alex (Redwood): I'll loop in our compliance lead. Expect an email and the standard pilot DPA attachment.
[11:47] Sarah (BrightByte): Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[11:49] Alex (Redwood): Thanks — we'll follow up with the docs and the meeting notes. end.
